title: Mechanisms of HSV-1 helicase-primase inhibition and replication fork complex assembly
abstract: Herpesviruses are widespread double-stranded DNA viruses that establish lifelong latency and cause various diseases. Although DNA-polymerase-targeting antivirals are effective, increasing drug resistance underscores the need for alternatives. Helicase-primase inhibitors (HPIs) are promising antivirals, but their mechanisms of action are poorly defined. Furthermore, how the helicase-primase (H/P) complex and DNA polymerase coordinate genome replication is not well understood for herpesviruses. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the herpes simplex virus 1 H/P complex bound to HPIs, showing that these lock the H/P complex in an inactive state. Single-molecule assays reveal that HPIs cause H/P complexes to pause in unwinding activity on DNA. The structure of an HPI-bound replication fork complex, comprising the H/P complex (UL5, UL52, and UL8) and the polymerase holoenzyme (UL30 and UL42), reveals a previously uncharacterized interface bridging these complexes. These findings provide a structural framework for understanding herpesvirus replisome assembly and advancing inhibitor development.

Full narrative

Mechanisms of HSV-1 helicase-primase inhibition and replication fork complex assembly addresses a central problem in herpesvirus therapeutics: how helicase-primase inhibitors work, and how the viral replication machinery is organized around that target. Published in Cell in 2025, the paper sits at the intersection of viral replication, DNA replication, replisome biology, and antiviral development, with funding support from sources including the Burroughs Wellcome Fund, NIAID, NIH, the National Cancer Institute, Servier, and the Broad Institute.

The clearest impact signal so far is scholarly reuse. The article has 6 citations, all recorded in 2026, indicating that it is still in the early stages of its citation life but is already being taken up by subsequent work. The citing literature is highly relevant to the paper’s topic, with recurring emphasis on herpesvirus infections and treatments, cytomegalovirus and broader herpesvirus research, and related questions in viral replication and protein structure.

That uptake is visible in the venues and directions of the citing work. The paper is referenced in Nature, Antiviral Research, Acta Pharmaceutica Sinica B, Expert Opinion on Therapeutic Patents, and two bioRxiv preprints, suggesting that its relevance spans basic structural virology, translational antiviral research, and drug-development discussions. Several citing works are explicitly about helicase-primase inhibitors, herpes simplex virus susceptibility, and herpesvirus replication machinery, which is consistent with the article’s mechanistic focus.
